articles.title: CPU vs GPU: Why Computers Use Two Kinds of Processor
articles.excerpt: A CPU has a few strong cores that finish tasks quickly; a GPU has many simpler cores that work on huge amounts of data at once. Here is how they differ and cooperate.
blocks: A CPU (central processing unit) and a GPU (graphics processing unit) are both chips that do calculations, but they are built for different jobs. A CPU has a small number of strong cores and is designed to finish each task quickly. A GPU has a very large number of simpler cores and is designed to push a lot of similar work through at the same time. Most computers, phones and servers use both, and each does the work it suits best.

The CPU is the main processor of a computer. According to Wikipedia's article on the subject, it runs the instructions of a program and performs the arithmetic, logic, control and input/output operations those instructions ask for. Inside it, an arithmetic logic unit does the sums and bit-level logic, registers hold the numbers being worked on, and a control unit directs the steps.

Those steps repeat in a loop called the instruction cycle. The CPU fetches the next instruction from memory, decodes it to see what operation it asks for, and executes it. The result goes to a register or back to memory, and the cycle begins again. Because a program often has to make decisions along the way (if this, then that), CPUs include complex control logic for branching and scheduling.

CPUs also carry caches, small and very fast memories close to each core that keep copies of data used often. Modern chips usually have several levels: a small, fast L1 cache per core, a larger L2, and a larger L3 that cores typically share. A multi-core CPU puts several cores on one chip so it can run several threads or programs at once. GeeksforGeeks puts typical CPU core counts at roughly 4 to 64.

A GPU began as a chip for graphics. Wikipedia describes it as a specialised circuit designed to accelerate computer graphics and image processing. Drawing a scene on a screen means working out the colour of millions of pixels, and the calculation for one pixel is largely independent of the next. That makes the job easy to split across many small calculation units, and modern GPUs have, in Wikipedia's words, hundreds or thousands of them.

Intel's comparison page describes the GPU's style as parallel: it divides work across many cores at once. Each core is simpler than a CPU core, and the control logic and caches are smaller. Instead of relying on big caches, GPUs rely on high memory bandwidth, meaning they can move large amounts of data in and out quickly. Problems that split neatly into many identical pieces are sometimes called "embarrassingly parallel", and they are where GPUs shine.

Two words help here. Latency is how long one task takes from start to finish. Throughput is how much total work gets done in a given time. A CPU is tuned for low latency: when you click a button, you want that one action handled at once. A GPU is tuned for high throughput: when you draw a frame, you want millions of small calculations done together, and it matters little how long any single one takes.

CPU: few strong cores, complex control logic, large caches, good at varied and step-by-step tasks
GPU: many simple cores, simpler control logic, high memory bandwidth, good at repeating the same operation on lots of data

According to Intel, CPUs handle running the operating system and programs, web browsing, spreadsheets, databases and game physics calculations. GPUs handle rendering graphics in games, video editing and AI workloads. GeeksforGeeks adds matrix and vector maths and image processing to the GPU list.

The AI link is worth a closer look. Training and running neural networks involves enormous amounts of multiplication and addition on grids of numbers, called matrices. Wikipedia notes that GPUs are increasingly used for artificial intelligence because they accelerate this kind of linear algebra, and that Nvidia added dedicated Tensor cores for deep learning in its Turing design in 2018.
From graphics chip to general-purpose helper

Early graphics chips were fixed in what they could do. Over time they became programmable. Wikipedia's timeline mentions Texas Instruments' TMS34010 in 1986 as described as the first fully programmable graphics processor, and Nvidia's CUDA platform in 2007 as the earliest widely adopted model for general-purpose computing on a GPU. Using a GPU for tasks other than graphics is called GPGPU. Wikipedia gives the protein-folding project Folding@home as an example, saying it can run up to forty times faster on GPUs than on CPUs in some circumstances.
A GPU is not simply a faster CPU. For a task that must run one step after another, with each step depending on the last, extra GPU cores add little.

In a typical program the CPU is in charge. It runs the main logic, prepares the data and hands the heavy, repetitive part to the GPU. The GPU does its calculation and returns the result. Intel's page concludes that the question is no longer CPU versus GPU, because most workloads benefit from both.

Chip makers also combine the two. Some CPUs include a GPU on the same chip for built-in graphics, which suits laptops, tablets and phones where size and energy use matter, according to Intel. Others add a neural processing unit (NPU), a block designed to help with AI inference, the stage where an already trained model makes predictions. A separate, discrete graphics card adds more parallel power when a task needs it.

Because the designs differ, comparing a CPU's core count with a GPU's is not meaningful. A GPU core is far simpler, so thousands of them are not the same as thousands of CPU cores. GPU speed is often quoted in teraflops (trillions of floating-point operations per second), which Wikipedia describes as an estimate. A figure like this says little about how a chip will perform on a specific program. General information only; check independent test results for the workload you care about.

sources.title: Difference between CPU and GPU, GeeksforGeeks

articles.title: What Is Training Data? How AI Learns From Examples
articles.excerpt: Training data is the set of examples a machine-learning model learns from. Learn about labels, supervised and unsupervised learning, and why test data is kept apart.
blocks: Training data is the collection of examples a machine-learning model is shown while it learns. The model is not given a list of rules. It adjusts its internal settings, called parameters, so that its outputs match the patterns in the examples. What the data contains, how it is labelled and how it is kept separate from the data used for testing all shape how well the finished model works.

DataCamp defines labelled data as raw data that has been assigned one or more labels to add context or meaning. Each example pairs an input with a known answer. In a spam filter, emails are tagged as spam or not spam. In speech recognition, audio is paired with a written transcript. In medical imaging, scans are labelled with the correct diagnosis, and for driving systems, images are marked with objects such as pedestrians and other vehicles.

Toloka, a data-labelling company, calls these labels "ground truth": the answer the model is trying to predict. The model makes a prediction, compares it with the label and adjusts to reduce the error. This approach is called supervised learning.

Unlabelled data is raw data with no tags. It is usually much easier and cheaper to collect, but the model gets no answer key. In unsupervised learning, the model looks for structure on its own. Toloka lists clustering (grouping similar items) and association (finding things that tend to occur together) as typical methods, with uses such as grouping customers by buying habits or spotting unusual transactions.

There are middle paths. Toloka describes a hybrid approach in which automated methods propose labels and people review and correct them, trading some accuracy for lower cost. Wikipedia's article on data sets notes that the exact methods vary with the problem and the amount of data available.

Supervised learning: labelled examples, predicts a known kind of answer (a category or a number)
Unsupervised learning: unlabelled examples, finds groups and patterns without being told what to look for

DataCamp points out that labelling is slow and costly, especially for specialised material like radiology images that may need expert knowledge. People make mistakes, and different annotators can apply different standards. In niche fields, labelled data can be scarce. Toloka adds that labels can carry bias and may expose sensitive information.

These weaknesses pass into the model. If labels are inconsistent, the model learns inconsistent behaviour. If the examples cover some situations far more than others, the model will do better on the common ones. Neither source claims any model is free of this, and it is one reason people examine what data went into a system.
Wikipedia explains that data used to build a model is usually split into three sets, each with a different job.

Training set: the examples used to fit the model's parameters, such as the connection weights in a neural network
Validation set: examples used to tune settings chosen by the builder (for instance the number of hidden units) and to compare candidate models
Test set: data kept apart from training, used at the end to judge how well the final model works on new examples

The reason for the split is overfitting. A model can learn quirks of its training examples that do not hold in general, a bit like a student memorising past exam answers. Wikipedia says that a model that fits the training or validation data much better than the test data is likely overfitted. It also says the test set should never be used to train the model or fine-tune its settings, otherwise it no longer gives an honest check. Where data is scarce, builders may use cross-validation, which rotates which part of the data is held back.
Terminology is not fully consistent. Wikipedia notes that "validation" and "test" are sometimes swapped in the literature, so check how a given paper or product defines them.

Chatbots built on large language models are trained on very large amounts of text, much of which has no human-written label. The usual trick is that the text supplies its own answer: the model sees part of a passage and learns to predict what comes next. The sources used for this article do not cover those systems in detail, so this paragraph is a general outline only. Companies differ in what they say about their data, and many do not publish full details.

A model can only learn what its examples show. More examples, better labels and a fair, held-back test set usually make for a more trustworthy result, while gaps and errors in the data show up later as gaps and errors in the output. When you read that a system was "trained on" something, the useful follow-up questions are what the data was, who labelled it, and how the maker checked the result on examples it had not seen.

sources.title: Understanding the difference between labeled and unlabeled data, Toloka
Training, validation, and test data sets, Wikipedia

articles.title: How a Quartz Watch Keeps Time With a Vibrating Crystal
articles.excerpt: A quartz watch counts the vibrations of a tiny crystal, usually 32,768 a second, and divides them down to one tick. Here is why that is so steady and how it can drift.
blocks: A quartz watch keeps time by counting the vibrations of a tiny piece of quartz crystal. In most watches the crystal vibrates 32,768 times a second. Electronics divide that number down until there is one pulse per second, and that pulse moves the hands or the digits. The method is steady because the crystal's rate barely changes, and because dividing a fast, stable vibration into slow ticks makes any small error tiny.
Why quartz can vibrate on command

Quartz is piezoelectric. According to Wikipedia, Jacques and Pierre Curie discovered this property in 1880. Squeezing or bending the crystal produces an electric charge, and applying an electric charge makes it flex. That two-way link lets a circuit drive the crystal and listen to it at the same time.

In a crystal oscillator, an amplifier sends its output through the quartz, which lets one frequency pass and filters out the rest. That frequency is fed back into the amplifier, so the circuit locks onto the crystal's natural rate. Wikipedia explains that in modern standard-quality quartz clocks the crystal is cut in the shape of a small tuning fork and trimmed so that it vibrates at 32,768 Hz. One hertz (Hz) is one vibration per second.

The number is not random. It is 2 to the power of 15, which means 15 simple divide-by-two circuits in a row turn it into exactly one pulse per second. Wikipedia adds that the figure is above the range of human hearing, yet low enough to keep power use, cost and size down. NIST, the United States national measurement institute, confirms in its timekeeping FAQ that a quartz crystal in a wristwatch circuit usually vibrates at 32,768 Hz and that the circuit divides by 32,768 to produce one-second ticks.

NIST gives a worked example. Suppose the crystal is off by 0.1 Hz. Because the watch has to count 32,768 vibrations for each second, it takes 327,680 seconds for that error to add up to one full second. That is about 0.26 seconds lost or gained per day. The higher the frequency being counted, the smaller each tick-sized error becomes.

The crystal vibrates at a steady rate, usually 32,768 Hz
A chain of dividers cuts that to 1 Hz
The 1 Hz pulse drives a small motor for the hands or updates a digital display

Wikipedia says standard 32,768 Hz resonators are warranted to about six parts per million over the long term at 31 degrees Celsius. That is roughly 15 seconds per 30 days. Higher-grade movements can do much better: Wikipedia lists ±1 to ±25 seconds per year for high-accuracy movements, and notes that watches certified by the Swiss COSC chronometer test are allowed ±25.55 seconds per year at 23 degrees Celsius.

For comparison, NIST says a 1 GHz atomic clock off by 1 Hz would lose one second in about 31.7 years. Atomic clocks operate at far higher precision and are a different class of device from a wristwatch crystal.
What makes a quartz watch drift

Temperature is the main cause. The crystal's rate changes slightly as it warms or cools. Wikipedia gives the figures: a deviation of 1 degree Celsius from the ideal costs about 0.035 parts per million, which is around 1.1 seconds a year, while a deviation of 10 degrees costs about 3.5 parts per million, around 110 seconds a year. Consumer crystals work best at roughly 25 to 28 degrees Celsius. Wikipedia points out that a watch worn on the wrist stays close to body temperature, so the case acts as a small "crystal oven" that lessens big swings.

Ageing of the crystal and the tuning of the individual watch also play a part. Many quartz watches have a small adjustment inside, and some more expensive ones measure temperature and correct for it. The sources used here do not say how common that feature is.
Quartz watches are not rated by how much they drift in a day but in seconds per month or year. A watch that is a minute off after a year is behaving normally for a standard model.

According to Wikipedia, the first quartz clock was built at Bell Telephone Laboratories in October 1927 by Joseph W. Horton and Warren A. Marrison, and was accurate to about 0.01 second per day. It filled a room's worth of equipment rather than a wrist. In December 1969 Seiko produced the first commercial quartz wristwatch, the Quartz-Astron 35SQ, which Wikipedia says used an 8,192 Hz oscillator and was accurate to 0.2 seconds a day, about one minute a year. Later watches settled on 32,768 Hz.

Today the same idea sits in many devices. Computers, microcontrollers and household appliances often contain a small 32,768 Hz crystal to keep a clock running, though the sources here are about watches and do not list specific devices.

articles.title: What Refresh Rate Means: 60Hz, 120Hz and Beyond
articles.excerpt: Refresh rate is how many times per second a screen updates its picture. See how it differs from frame rate, what common figures mean, and what variable refresh rate does.
blocks: Refresh rate is the number of times per second a screen shows a new image, measured in hertz (Hz). A 60Hz screen updates 60 times a second and a 120Hz screen 120 times. A higher number allows smoother motion, but only if the content being shown actually has enough frames to use it.

These two terms are easy to mix up. Refresh rate belongs to the display: how often it can put up a new picture. Frame rate belongs to the source: how many images a game, film or video produces each second, usually written as frames per second (fps). Wikipedia's article on refresh rate stresses that the two can differ. Display Ninja puts it plainly: a higher refresh rate lets a display handle a higher frame rate, but does nothing if the source never goes above the display's current rate.
Samsung's monitor guide makes the same point: if a system cannot consistently produce enough frames to match the monitor, you may not see much improvement.

Wikipedia lists common monitor refresh rates of 50, 60, 75, 100, 120, 144, 200 and 240 Hz. Samsung names 60, 120, 144, 240 and 360 Hz as common. Televisions were long built around 60 Hz in regions that used the NTSC standard and 50 Hz where PAL or SECAM was used, and Wikipedia says many high-end LCD TVs now use 120 or 240 Hz (100 or 200 Hz in the 50 Hz regions).

A little arithmetic shows what the number means for timing. At 60Hz a new picture can appear every 16.7 milliseconds (1000 divided by 60). At 120Hz it is every 8.3 milliseconds, and at 240Hz every 4.2 milliseconds.
Flicker on old and new screens

On old cathode-ray tube (CRT) monitors, Wikipedia explains, the glowing coating fades quickly, so the screen must be redrawn constantly, and a low rate produces visible flicker and eye strain. It says smaller CRT monitors are comfortable at 60 to 72 Hz and about 100 Hz is comfortable at almost any size.

Liquid-crystal (LCD) pixels hold their state while powered, so Wikipedia says there is no inherent flicker at any refresh rate. Here the refresh rate instead limits how fast the image can change and the highest frame rate that can be displayed.

Samsung says a higher number means smoother transitions and less blur, especially with fast-moving content. Display Ninja calls the step from 60Hz to 120Hz or 144Hz very noticeable in gaming, and notes that a higher refresh rate can lower display latency even when the game runs at 60 fps or less. The gains shrink at the top end, since the source has no frames beyond what the game produces.

Ordinary video: Display Ninja notes that 24 fps films and 60 fps online video do not need a 120, 144 or 240Hz display
Games that run at or below 60 fps: a faster screen adds little
Software that makes extra frames for video (interpolation): some viewers find the result looks artificial

A fixed-rate screen can show "tearing" when the source delivers a frame partway through a refresh: part of the picture comes from one frame and part from the next. Variable refresh rate (VRR) lets the display change its rate on the fly to match what the source delivers. Wikipedia names AMD's FreeSync and Nvidia's G-Sync as implementations, and says VRR can save power and cut input latency in games. Samsung and Display Ninja both say these systems reduce tearing and stutter.

Samsung's guide, which is from a monitor maker and should be read as such, suggests 60Hz for everyday tasks such as browsing and documents, 75 to 120Hz for smoother video and action-heavy content, and 100Hz or higher for video editing and content creation. For gaming it suggests 100 to 120Hz for casual players on a budget, 144 to 200Hz for most gamers and 240 to 360Hz for competitive players. These are the company's recommendations, not fixed rules, and the right choice depends on the games, the graphics hardware and the budget.

Check the whole chain. The computer, the cable or port and the monitor settings all have to support a higher rate before the screen will use it. The sources used here do not cover cable limits, so check your device's manual.
In short: refresh rate is how quickly the screen can update, frame rate is how quickly the content is made, and the smoothness you see is limited by the lower of the two.

sources.title: Everything you need to know about monitor refresh rates, Samsung

articles.title: How Contrails Form Behind Aeroplanes at High Altitude
articles.excerpt: Contrails are lines of ice crystals that form when water vapour from jet exhaust meets very cold air. Learn why some vanish quickly and others spread for hours.
blocks: A contrail is a line of ice crystals that forms behind an aircraft flying high in very cold air. The name is short for "condensation trail". Water vapour in the engine exhaust cools, turns to droplets and freezes. Whether the trail vanishes in seconds or stretches across the sky for hours depends mainly on how humid the surrounding air is.

According to Wikipedia, engine exhaust is mostly water vapour and carbon dioxide. At cruising height it enters air that is extremely cold. The extra vapour raises the humidity in that small patch of air to saturation, so the vapour condenses into tiny droplets, which freeze if it is cold enough. Soot and sulphur compounds in the exhaust give the vapour something to condense on.

The trail does not start right at the engine. The exhaust takes a little time to mix with the cold air and cool, so the visible trail begins a short distance behind the aircraft. NOAA's description agrees on the basic process: vapour in the exhaust cools, condenses and freezes into ice crystals that form a visible trail, when the added vapour pushes already moist air to saturation.

Contrails usually form above about 8,000 metres (26,000 feet), where the air is colder than about minus 36.5 degrees Celsius, says Wikipedia. NOAA likewise cites a cruising altitude of 26,000 feet or higher for most commercial jets in this context. Contrails can also form lower down if the air is cold and moist enough. Other sources quote slightly different temperature thresholds, so treat the numbers as approximate.
Why some trails vanish and others stay

Wikipedia says that, depending on temperature and humidity, a contrail may last for seconds or minutes, or persist for hours and spread several kilometres wide, eventually resembling natural cirrus or altocumulus cloud. NOAA's material points to the same ingredient: higher relative humidity means a contrail lasts longer, and wind affects how fast it spreads.

Dry air around the aircraft: the ice crystals evaporate quickly and the trail is short
Air already humid enough to hold ice: the crystals persist and can grow as they attract more moisture
Wind: stretches and spreads a persistent trail

The crystals in a persistent trail keep collecting water vapour from the surrounding moist air, which is why they can grow and fan out. NOAA adds that the amount of supersaturation (air holding more moisture than it normally could) affects how dense or thick the trail looks.
A useful clue about the air

Because the length of a trail reflects how humid the upper air is, people watching the sky sometimes use contrails as a rough hint about the weather. The sources used here describe the physics but do not make forecasting claims, so this is an observation rather than a rule.

This is an area of active research. Wikipedia reports that persistent contrails add to cloudiness and that their net radiative forcing is roughly 0.03 to 0.06 watts per square metre, because they trap outgoing heat more than they reflect incoming sunlight. It adds that their warming effect may be similar in size to that of aviation's carbon dioxide emissions, depending on the time span used, and that they tend to cool daytime temperatures and warm those at night.

Rerouting a small share of flights around the most contrail-prone air has been suggested as a way to cut the effect. Wikipedia also mentions a German study from November 2025 which concluded that the climate impact of contrails cannot yet be estimated well enough to justify rerouting strategies. In other words, the size of the effect is still being worked out.

Contrails are made of water ice formed from the exhaust vapour. The sources used here describe a physical process of condensation and freezing and do not support other explanations sometimes offered online.

Hot exhaust adds water vapour to very cold air
The vapour condenses on tiny particles and freezes into ice crystals
Dry surroundings make the trail short; humid ones let it last and spread
Persistent contrails add cloud, and scientists are still working out how much they matter for the climate

Next time a bright line appears behind a distant aircraft, the way it behaves tells you something about the air up there at that moment, even though you cannot see the temperature or humidity directly.
